name: Cetyl tranexamate mesylate

lead: Cetyl tranexamate mesylate is a modified form of tranexamic acid made for skincare. People use it in serums aimed at dark spots, uneven tone and post-acne marks.

Tranexamic acid is thought to reduce the signalling that drives melanocyte pigment production, and the cetyl chain makes the molecule more fat-soluble so it can cross the skin barrier better than the parent compound. A 2021 study in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology examined its skin-lightening performance on sun-damaged skin, and a small registered trial looked at acne-related hyperpigmentation.

paras: It is applied as a leave-on serum or cream, usually daily and often with sunscreen, since sun exposure drives pigmentation. It is commonly combined with other brightening ingredients. Fading of marks is judged over weeks to months.
Sources reviewed report no specific safety concerns, but long-term data are lacking. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient; as with any topical, irritation is possible.

angle.text: Cetyl tranexamate mesylate is a fat-soluble tranexamic acid form used in serums to reduce pigment production, so dark spots fade and tone looks more even. Published data include a 2021 cosmetic-dermatology study and a small registered trial.

lead: Cetyl tranexamate mesylate is a lipophilic derivative of tranexamic acid, formulated as a cosmetic ingredient for topical skin-lightening products. It is the cetyl ester of tranexamic acid supplied as a mesylate salt. People use serums containing it to fade dark spots, even out skin tone and calm redness, with the aim of a more uniform, brighter complexion.[1]

Tranexamic acid itself is a hydrophilic zwitterionic molecule that is described as penetrating the stratum corneum poorly; formulators have used penetration enhancers, microneedling or lipophilic derivatives such as cetyl tranexamate mesylate to address this.[2] An in vivo Raman spectroscopy study of an ester-modified tranexamic acid ingredient reported 2.1- and 3.8-fold higher skin absorption than free tranexamic acid at 3% and 1%.[3]

Published human evidence is limited and largely from the ingredient's supplier. In a 2021 study of a serum with 2.0% cetyl tranexamate mesylate, 35 women applying it twice daily for 8 weeks showed falls of 16.9% in melanin index and 34.3% in erythema index, with no questionable adverse reactions in a 54-person patch test.[3] A small registered trial also examined its effect on acne-related hyperpigmentation.[4]

paras: It is used in leave-on serums and creams aimed at dark spots, melasma-like discoloration and post-acne marks. The rationale is that attaching a cetyl (long fatty) chain makes the molecule more lipophilic than tranexamic acid, which may improve delivery through the skin barrier.[2] A related ester, tranexamic acid cetyl ester hydrochloride, has been described in Japanese quasi-drug products for melasma, and a 2008 patent application from a cosmetics company covered topical compositions with a tranexamic acid ester.[3]

Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic; its proposed skin-lightening action involves reducing plasmin-related signalling that stimulates melanocytes.[2] The cetyl ester is presented as a topical delivery form of this approach. A 2024 narrative review of tranexamic acid for hyperpigmentation beyond melasma, covering oral, topical, intradermal and microneedling routes, noted that most such uses are off-label.[3] Detailed pharmacokinetic data for the derivative itself are not available.

The 2021 report in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology tested a facial serum with 2.0% cetyl tranexamate mesylate: safety by a modified repeat insult patch test in 54 people, and performance in 35 women applying it twice daily for 8 weeks, with reported reductions of 16.9% in melanin index and 34.3% in erythema index and subject-reported improvements from week 2. All authors were affiliated with the ingredient's supplier.[1][3]

A separate registered study (NCT06080035), completed with 22 participants and started in November 2023, examined effects on the appearance of acne-related post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation; it is listed as a non-randomised study.[4]

For topical tranexamic acid in general, a 2021 network meta-analysis of 14 melasma therapies ranked it mid-to-low for efficacy with a relatively high side-effect rate, and a 2022 review found microneedling improved melasma beyond topical therapy alone.[3] A general reference notes that efficacy for melasma remained unproven as of 2017.[2] Larger independent randomised trials of the cetyl ester have not been identified.
The supplier study reported no questionable adverse reactions in a patch test of 54 people.[3] Long-term data are not available. As with any topical product, irritation is possible.
